client: I’ve been feeling really overwhelmed since starting this new job at the tech startup. Last week, I missed an important deadline, and now I’m constantly worried I’m not performing well enough. I’m not sure if therapy can really help with this—it feels like the pressure is just part of the job, and I don’t know if I can handle it.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy weight of expectations and self-doubt since joining this new work environment. I hear how distressing it feels when you fall short of a deadline and how that's shaken your confidence. What thoughts come up for you when you notice this worry about not performing well enough?

client: My mind just keeps racing with thoughts like "Everyone else is handling this fine" and "They're going to realize they made a mistake hiring me." It's exhausting because even when I complete tasks, I second-guess if they're good enough. I don't know how to quiet these thoughts—they feel so true in the moment.
therapist: Those thoughts sound really persistent and convincing, especially when they come with that exhausting cycle of second-guessing your work. It might help to explore where these beliefs about others "handling it fine" come from—have you noticed any evidence that contradicts these thoughts?

client: Well, I did overhear my coworker telling our manager he was struggling with his workload last week. But that just makes me think - if he's admitting it, he must actually be doing better than me. I'm the only one who can't seem to keep up without falling apart. It's like everyone else is coping, even when they say they're not.
therapist: I notice how quickly your mind turns even evidence of others struggling into proof that you're somehow falling short. That pattern of negative self-comparison sounds very painful—what do you imagine might happen if you allowed yourself the same compassion you'd give to that coworker who admitted he was struggling?

client: I guess if I showed myself that same compassion, I might feel less pressure and maybe even perform better. But it's hard because I feel like I should be stronger than this—like admitting I'm struggling would make me look weak or incapable. I don't want to be the person who can't handle the job.
therapist: You're holding onto this belief that strength means never struggling, which adds another layer of pressure to an already difficult situation. I wonder what it would feel like to challenge that assumption—have you ever admired someone who showed vulnerability while still being clearly capable at their job?

client: Actually, my last manager at my previous job was open about when she was overwhelmed, and I respected her more for it. But I don't know if I can be like that—I feel like I haven't earned that right yet since I'm still new. What if people just see it as me not being cut out for this role?
therapist: It's interesting how you could admire that quality in your manager while feeling it's not accessible to you yet—that double standard you're holding yourself to sounds exhausting. What do you imagine might need to change for you to feel you've "earned" the right to be human in this new role?

client: I guess I'd need to prove myself by succeeding perfectly for... I don't know how long. Maybe six months? But that seems impossible when I'm already struggling in week three. It's like I've set this unrealistic standard where I can't show any weakness until I'm some fantasy version of a perfect employee. Even saying that out loud makes me realize how unfair it is.
therapist: It sounds like you're starting to recognize how this "perfect employee" standard you've created might be setting you up for disappointment before you've even had a chance to grow into the role. What might it feel like to shift that expectation from needing to be perfect to allowing yourself to learn and develop over time?

client: It feels scary to shift that expectation because I worry people will judge me if I don't have everything figured out right away. But I guess it might feel freeing to allow myself some room to learn—it's just hard to trust that others will see it that way too. I keep imagining them thinking I'm not good enough if I'm not perfect from the start.
therapist: That fear of being judged makes so much sense—it's like you're anticipating others' criticism before they even have a chance to form an opinion. I wonder if we could explore what it might look like to balance that worry with the possibility that others might actually appreciate seeing your authentic growth process?

client: I can see how anticipating criticism might be making things harder for me, but it's difficult to imagine others appreciating my growth process. I'm so focused on not failing that I forget people might actually value honesty and effort over perfection. Still, it feels risky to let my guard down—what if I'm wrong and they do judge me?
therapist: You're recognizing this important tension—the possibility that growth could be valued versus the very real fear of judgment. What small step could you imagine taking that might test this belief, while still feeling safe enough for you?

client: Maybe I could admit to my manager that I'm still getting up to speed on certain tasks—I just worry they'll think less of me if I do. It feels safer to pretend I have everything under control, even though I know that's not true. I guess part of me thinks honesty might backfire and confirm their doubts about me.
therapist: It sounds like you're weighing the risks between being authentic versus maintaining this protective façade of control—that's such an important awareness. What do you imagine might be different if you approached this conversation as someone actively learning rather than someone "failing to know"?

client: If I framed it as actively learning, maybe my manager would see it as a sign of commitment and willingness to grow—not failure. But it's still hard to shake the fear that they'll think less of me, especially since I'm so new. I guess I'm worried they'll question why they hired me in the first place.
therapist: You're touching on something really important—how our fear of being "found out" can make us forget that every new hire goes through a learning period. That shift from "I should know everything" to "I'm committed to learning" sounds significant—what might help you hold onto that perspective when the self-doubt creeps back in?
